source.title: Provable Benefit of Orthogonal Initialization in Optimizing Deep Linear Networks
source.authors: Wei Hu; Lechao Xiao; Jeffrey Pennington

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study proves and experimentally examines how orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization affects gradient-descent convergence in deep linear networks. This tests initialization and training speed using a different model class from V4's stated plain nonlinear networks.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR classification-error versions, local-minima version, shortcut version, above-stability learning-rate version, and batch-normalization version are not tested. The paper's cited results about nonlinear networks are prior work, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests V4's general connection between initialization, convergence speed and trainable depth using proofs and synthetic experiments in plain deep linear networks. It does not test V4's specific nonlinear, tanh or convolutional results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: orthogonal initialization guarantees efficient convergence with a sufficient width independent of depth, while Gaussian initialization incurs exponentially long convergence times at sufficiently sublinear widths under the stated assumptions. These are results for deep linear networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and trains deep linear networks with gradient descent and orthogonal or Gaussian initialization. V4 concerns activation-matched initialization in plain nonlinear networks and orthogonal convolution kernels.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scheme and the width-to-depth relationship change convergence; the paper reports orthogonal width requirements independent of depth and Gaussian requirements that scale nearly linearly with depth.
record.problems: The theoretical results are for deep linear networks and squared loss. Experiments use a fixed synthetic dataset; plotted values are not numerically reported in the text, and no experimental uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: Convolutional classification on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted labels, SGD/Adam, and model-size or regularization effects on training classification error.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Training degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization and Fixup.

Activation-specific comparisons in nonlinear networks; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization in very deep tanh networks; orthogonal convolution kernels and training at 10,000 layers. The empirical setting here is synthetic linear regression.
Above-threshold learning rates, catapult recovery, curvature trajectories, edge-of-stability behavior and divergence below the initial threshold.
Batch-normalization comparisons, accuracy gain, higher learning-rate tolerance and Fixup residual networks.

missing.what: The proof bounds normalized singular values of partial weight products between 0.9 and 1.1 throughout training under orthogonal initialization, directly connecting preserved signal propagation to convergence.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source listed for V4. Gaussian stalls support the initialization contrast and do not warrant a limits_scope verdict. The untested nonlinear settings likewise do not warrant limits_scope. The experimental widths can be below dx=1024, so those experiments should not be described as directly satisfying Theorem 4.1's width assumptions.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, and early stopping.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual nonlinear networks, batch normalization, shortcuts, ImageNet/CIFAR-10, and Fixup.
Activation-matched initializations in nonlinear plain networks; tanh and convolutional networks, including 10,000-layer networks. This paper tests deep linear networks.
Learning rates above stability limits, loss-curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence.
Batch normalization, accuracy gain, learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual networks.

rows.subject: deep linear network with orthogonal initialization
rows.size_stated: hidden width m satisfying (5), with m ≥ dx; depth L
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent from independently sampled scaled orthogonal weights; theorem gives convergence to a global minimum.

conditions.value: m ≥ C·r̃κ²dy(1 + ||W*||²) + log(r/δ), and m ≥ dx

rows.measure: Excess squared training loss over the global minimum
rows.value: With probability at least 1 − δ, loss decreases geometrically: `(ℓ(t) − ℓ*) ≤ (1 − ηLλr(XᵀX)/(2dy))^t (ℓ(0) − ℓ*)`
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − δ over random initialization; theorem uses O(·) bounds
rows.note: The theorem states the sufficient width condition need not depend on depth L. This is a squared-loss convergence result on a deep linear network, not a classification benchmark.
rows.check: Correct the width condition to m ≥ C·r̃κ²[dy(1 + ||W*||²) + log(r/δ)], with m ≥ dx and the setup's m ≥ max{dx,dy}. The logarithmic term is inside the multiplied bracket. The baseline is the global minimum ℓ*, not an unspecified baseline.

rows.subject: deep linear network with Gaussian initialization
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent from independent Gaussian weights, under the stated initialization scaling assumptions.
rows.measure: Squared training objective during the initial iterations
rows.value: With probability at least 0.9, for the first e^(Ω(L^γ)) iterations the objective is between 0.4||Y||²F and 0.6||Y||²F
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 0.9 over random initialization; asymptotic bounds in L
rows.note: This gives a contrast with orthogonal initialization under the theorem's width, depth, and learning-rate conditions; it establishes a long stall interval, not failure to converge forever.
rows.check: The Gaussian stall supports the initialization contrast in V4; it is not a partial occurrence of that contrast. The optimum is zero, whereas loss remains between 0.4||Y||²F and 0.6||Y||²F for exponentially many iterations. This establishes a finite stall, not permanent failure.

source_check.correct: The optimal objective is explicitly 0 under Y = W*X. With probability at least 0.9, the objective remains between 0.4||Y||²F and 0.6||Y||²F for the first exp(Ω(L^γ)) iterations under Theorem 5.1's assumptions.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5 opening assumptions and Theorem 5.1, p. 6.
source_check.problem: The text supplies the optimum, so baseline 'not stated' is incorrect.

rows.subject: family of linear networks
rows.operation_detail: Swept depth and width under Gaussian and orthogonal initialization on a fixed synthetic dataset.
rows.note: Text reports a sharp trainable-to-untrainable transition: for Gaussian initialization its contour is characterized by a linear relation between width and depth; for orthogonal initialization the transition width is approximately independent of depth. Exact plotted values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Section 6 explicitly describes the initialization-dependent transition, so its qualitative direction is determinable without exact plotted values. Figure 1 displays log relative loss: the Gaussian transition follows a linear width-depth contour, while the orthogonal transition width is approximately independent of depth.

relationships.condition: Deep linear networks satisfying the respective orthogonal and Gaussian theorem assumptions
relationships.reason: R1 proves geometric convergence with a depth-independent sufficient width; R2 proves exponentially long Gaussian stalls when maximum layer width grows as O(L^(1−γ)). Both support the predicted initialization advantage.
relationships.display_finding: Under the respective theorem assumptions, orthogonal initialization guaranteed geometric convergence at a depth-independent sufficient width, whereas Gaussian initialization stalled exponentially long when maximum width grew as O(L^(1−γ)).
